title: Units, Dimensions and Vectors — NIOS Official Summary
intro: This is the NIOS Senior Secondary Physics (312) Learner's Guide summary for Lesson 1: Units, Dimensions and Vectors. It covers the scope of physics, the SI system of units, significant figures, dimensional analysis, and the basics of vectors — scalar versus vector quantities, vector addition by the triangle law, and the scalar and vector products.

sections.heading: Physics: Scope and Excitement
bullets: The scope of Physics is very wide and it covers a vast variety of natural phenomena.
It includes the study of mechanics, heat and thermodynamics, optics, waves and oscillations, electricity and magnetism, atomic and nuclear physics, electronics and communication.
The laws of physics are expressed in terms of physical quantities such as distance, speed, time, force, volume, electric current, etc.
For measurement, each physical quantity is assigned a unit.

sections.heading: The SI Units
bullets: The name SI is an abbreviation for Système International d'Unités — the International System of units.

The seven SI base quantities and units are: Length (metre, m); Mass (kilogram, kg); Time (second, s); Electric current (ampere, A); Temperature (kelvin, K); Luminous intensity (candela, cd); Amount of substance (mole, mol).
Mass: the SI unit of mass is the kilogram — the mass of a particular cylinder made of platinum-iridium alloy.
Length: the SI unit of length is the metre — defined as the distance travelled by light in vacuum in a time interval of 1/299792458 second.
Time: one second is defined as the time required for a Cesium-133 (133Cs) atom to undergo 9192631770 vibrations between two hyperfine levels of its ground state.

sections.heading: Significant Figures
bullets: Digits in a measurement that are known with certainty plus the first uncertain digit are called significant figures.
All non-zero digits are significant — for example, 315.58 has five significant figures.
All zeros between two non-zero digits are significant — for example, 5300405.003 has ten significant figures.
All zeros to the right of a decimal point AND to the right of a non-zero digit are significant — for example, 50.00 has four significant figures.
Zeros to the right of a decimal point but to the left of the first non-zero digit are NOT significant — for example, 0.00043 has only two significant figures.
In a whole number, all trailing zeros to the right of the last non-zero digit are not significant unless they come from a measurement (e.g. 5000 has one significant figure).

sections.heading: Dimensions and Dimensional Analysis
bullets: Derived units result from a mathematical combination of SI base units.
Applications of dimensions (or dimensional equations): derivation of a relationship between different physical quantities (or formula).
Checking up the accuracy of a formula (or relationship between different physical quantities).
Conversion of one system of units into another.
Derivation of units of a physical quantity.

sections.heading: Vectors and Scalars
bullets: A scalar quantity has only magnitude; no direction.
A vector quantity has both magnitude and direction.
A vector is represented by a line with an arrow indicating its direction (written as A with an arrow above).

Addition of vectors — triangle law: if two vectors are represented in magnitude and direction by the two sides of a triangle taken in order, the resultant is represented by the third side of the triangle taken in the opposite order. R = A + B.
Subtraction of vectors: R = A + (−B).

sections.heading: Multiplication of Vectors
bullets: Scalar (dot) product of two vectors A and B is written as A · B and is equal to AB cos θ, where θ is the angle between the vectors. The scalar product is a scalar quantity.
Vector (cross) product of two vectors A and B is written as A × B and has magnitude AB sin θ. The vector product is a vector quantity.
Unit vector: has unitary magnitude and a specified direction. It has no units and no dimensions. Â = A / |A|.

key_takeaways: Physical quantities are measured against units; the SI system has seven base units from which all others are derived.
Significant figures convey the precision of a measurement — non-zero digits and zeros between/right of decimal point of non-zero digits count.
Dimensional analysis can derive relationships, check formula accuracy and convert between unit systems.
A scalar has magnitude only; a vector has both magnitude and direction.
Vectors add by the triangle law (or equivalently the parallelogram law); they can be combined through scalar product (A · B = AB cos θ, a scalar) or vector product (|A × B| = AB sin θ, a vector).

glossary.definition: An abbreviation for Système International d'Unités — the internationally agreed system of units. There are seven base units in the SI system.
Digits in a measurement that are known with certainty plus the first uncertain digit; they convey the precision of the measurement.
An expression showing how a physical quantity is built up from the base quantities M (mass), L (length), T (time), A (current), etc., e.g. [M L T⁻²] for force.
A physical quantity that has only magnitude and no direction. Examples: mass, time, energy.
A physical quantity that has both magnitude and direction. Examples: displacement, velocity, force.
If two vectors are represented in magnitude and direction by the two sides of a triangle taken in order, the resultant is represented by the third side of the triangle taken in the opposite order.
A · B = AB cos θ. The scalar product of two vectors is itself a scalar quantity.
A × B has magnitude AB sin θ. The vector product of two vectors is itself a vector quantity, perpendicular to both A and B.
A vector of magnitude exactly one, used purely to indicate direction. It has no units and no dimensions.
